clue.text: Court serves claims, primarily making sound lawsuits with these

indicators.note: with these says the answer is what joins the initial to make the sound, so taking that initial away from the sound leaves the answer
sound means what is heard, so the word for lawsuits is written as it is pronounced, a hard opening consonant followed by the answer

parts.note: cases are lawsuits brought before a court

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of claims is used

parts.note: its first letter is C

explanation.surface: A legal scene: a court hands out writs, and claims lead to well-founded lawsuits.
explanation.walkthrough: Court here is a tennis court, and its serves are the definition. 'Claims, primarily' gives C, which 'with these' makes the 'sound' of CASES, written by ear as CACES; taking away the C leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis an ace is a serve the receiver cannot touch, so aces are winning serves on court.

clue.text: Blemish on this wobbly bottom of frequent flyer

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above, so the blemish word sits on top of what follows

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or blemish

indicators.note: wobbly means unsteady, so the letters of this are shaken into a new order
the bottom of a word in a down clue is its last letter

parts.note: its last letter is T

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark about a mark on the wobbly behind of someone who flies often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frequent flyer' looks like an air-miles phrase, but flyer alone is the definition, a bird. MAR sits 'on' SHTI ('wobbly' THIS), then the 'bottom of' frequent adds T.
explanation.definitionFit: The marsh tit is a small European songbird, so it is a flyer in the crossword sense of a bird.

clue.text: Ignoring the last perfect theory

indicators.note: To ignore the last of something is to leave it out, so the word's closing letter never reaches the grid.

parts.note: perfect is ideal, and the L on the end is left out

explanation.walkthrough: One letter separates the two words, which is why the sentence reads as an ordinary remark about a flawless theory rather than as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: theory → IDEA: both name a thought put up for consideration, with 'theory' the more formal of the two — an idea somebody has bothered to write down.

clue.text: First of cantilever bridges crossed having no parking inspectors

indicators.note: crossed means travelled over, so the bridges word spans the letter from cantilever, holding it inside
having no means the letter for parking is taken out

parts.note: spanners can mean things that span a gap, as bridges do
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

indicators.note: first of means just the opening letter is used

parts.note: its first letter is C

explanation.surface: An engineering scene: a cantilever bridge crossed by inspectors who find nowhere to park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having no' parking strips P from SPANNERS to give SANNERS, and 'crossed' sets C, the 'First of' cantilever, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Scanners are devices or people that examine things closely, as inspectors do.

clue.text: Pet Labrador's initially absent after eating posh food

indicators.note: A word's initial is the letter it starts with, so that one letter is what the clue is pointing at.
A word that is eating something has it inside, so these letters close round what comes next.
What is absent is not there at all, so the letter just named never appears in the word.

parts.note: to pet an animal is to fondle it
the first letter of LABRADOR, which is the one that goes missing
U is the crossword's shorthand for upper class, out of Nancy Mitford's U and non-U

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' is the verb, not the animal, and the surface's dog is there only so that a Labrador is standing by when the clue asks for a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: food → FONDUE: a fondue is the Swiss pot of melted cheese you dip bread into, so the general word defines it as one dish among many.

clue.text: Plant maybe in Spooner's garment dryer

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds of the two words are exchanged

parts.note: a sock is an item of clothing
a wringer squeezes water out of washing to dry it; said aloud, it begins with an R sound

explanation.surface: A household oddity: a plant growing in something used to dry clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks botanical but is Robert Plant of Led Zeppelin. SOCK WRINGER with its opening sounds swapped becomes the answer, since the W of wringer is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Plant, Led Zeppelin's frontman, is a famous example of a vocalist in a heavy band.

clue.text: Troops I fed left yankee wanting eggs

definitions.note: Caviar is a mass noun, one substance, where 'eggs' is plural. The two do not agree in number, but caviar is nothing except eggs, so the setter is allowed it.

indicators.note: Something fed into a word goes inside it, so the letter is dropped into the middle rather than added at either end.
A word wanting something does not have it, so the letters named are taken out.

parts.note: the cavalry are mounted troops
L is the abbreviation for left, and it is one of the two letters removed
Y is yankee in the NATO alphabet, and it goes as well
the letter is lifted straight out of the clue

explanation.walkthrough: The NATO alphabet is worth learning whole: yankee is Y, and any of its other letters can be asked for in exactly this way.
explanation.definitionFit: eggs → CAVIAR: caviar is the salted roe of the sturgeon, so the plain word names precisely what the delicacy is.

clue.text: Nice summer, fine at the beginning for festival

indicators.note: The letter named is wanted at the start, so it goes in front of everything else rather than after it.

parts.note: F is the pencil-maker's grade for fine
Nice is in France, and summer in French is été

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' with a capital N is the city, and once you see that, the clue is asking for a French word. A village fête is that same word borrowed back into English.
explanation.definitionFit: festival → FETE: a fête is the village fundraising day of stalls and raffles, which is a festival on a small and very English scale.

clue.text: Vegetable patch ardently covered

indicators.note: Something covered is out of sight under what lies on top of it, so the answer is buried in these words rather than spelt out by them.

parts.note: the run crosses the gap: the tail of 'patch' and the front of 'ardently'

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers are hardest to see when they straddle the gap between two words, and a gardening surface gives you no reason to go looking for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Vegetable → CHARD: chard is the leafy green grown for its thick white stalks, so the general word defines it as one vegetable among many.

clue.text: Sweet coke, hot drinks in cafe with espresso at first

indicators.note: To drink a thing in is to take it right inside you, so the shorter word disappears into the middle of the longer one.

parts.note: the first letter of CAFE, which leads off

indicators.note: Each word here is wanted only at its very start, so both hand over an opening letter and nothing else.

parts.note: the word is used as it stands, and it opens up to take something in
a coke is a cola, and it goes inside
the first letter of ESPRESSO, closing the answer off

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is something you could order at a counter, which is what hides the fact that two of them are wanted for one letter each.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet → CHOCOLATE: a chocolate is one of the sweets in the box, so the British word for confectionery defines it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Confirmed fronts of service uniforms dirty

indicators.note: The front of a word is where it begins, so each of the two words named hands over its opening letter and no more.

parts.note: the first letter of SERVICE
the first letter of UNIFORMS
dirty clothing is stained

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is courtroom English — what a judge says when an objection is upheld — while the surface stands in a barracks looking at somebody's kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Confirmed → SUSTAINED: an objection a judge sustains has been confirmed, and a claim sustained by evidence is one that has been borne out.

clue.text: Drunk Nelson at last provided English cutter

indicators.note: Whatever comes at last is the closing letter, and this one instruction is read back over two words in a row.

parts.note: the last letter of DRUNK
the last letter of NELSON
'provided that' and 'if' introduce the same condition
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.walkthrough: One instruction reaches back over two words at once, which is the step that hides the parse: 'Drunk Nelson at last' looks like a scene and is a pair of final letters.
explanation.definitionFit: cutter → KNIFE: a knife is the everyday tool for cutting, so the definition names it by the job rather than by the drawer it lives in.

clue.text: Extravagant Co-op surrounds home

indicators.note: To surround a thing is to close round it on both sides, so these letters split apart and take the rest inside.

parts.note: a coop is a cage for poultry, and here it opens up to take something in
over the top shortens to OTT

explanation.walkthrough: The Co-op of the surface is the grocer's; underneath it is a hen coop, and that pun is where all the clue's difficulty lives.
explanation.definitionFit: home → COTTAGE: a cottage is a small house in the country, so the plain word defines it as one kind of dwelling among many.

clue.text: Join firm, starts scared

indicators.note: Whichever piece starts is the one at the front, so the company goes in ahead of what the clue named first.

parts.note: CO is company, the standard two letters on a firm's name
to join two people in marriage is to wed them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' is the noun, not the adjective, and the surface's job offer is decoration — nothing in it has anything to do with fear.
explanation.definitionFit: scared → COWED: to be cowed is to be frightened into doing as you are told, so it is fear that has already changed how somebody behaves.

clue.text: Jews ask him a Zen problem

indicators.note: A problem is something crying out to be sorted out, and letters waiting to be sorted out are not yet in the right order.

parts.note: ten letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: A Zen problem is a koan, which is what holds the surface together. The answer names the Jews of central and eastern Europe, as against the Sephardim of Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Jews → ASHKENAZIM: the Hebrew plural names the Jewish communities of Germany and eastern Europe, so it defines one branch rather than the whole people.

clue.text: Sufferer I treated internally in a state

indicators.note: What happens internally happens inside, so the answer sits within these words instead of being built out of them.

parts.note: the run starts near the end of 'sufferer', crosses the whole of 'I', and continues into the front of 'treated'

explanation.walkthrough: The hidden run starts five letters into 'Sufferer' and crosses two gaps, and the medical surface is there to keep your eye travelling instead of looking.
explanation.definitionFit: a state → ERITREA: Eritrea is the country on the Red Sea that broke from Ethiopia in 1993, so 'state' here means a nation and not a mood.

clue.text: Bad religious scholar opens beer

indicators.note: To open a thing is to make a gap in it, and whatever makes the gap ends up inside.

parts.note: ale is beer, and it splits after its first letter
a Doctor of Divinity is a DD

explanation.walkthrough: DD for Doctor of Divinity is worth banking — crosswords reach for it whenever a churchman or a scholar turns up — and an addle egg is where the definition comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad → ADDLE: an addle egg is one that has gone rotten, and the word keeps that 'gone off' sense when it is applied to somebody's brains.

clue.text: View sample that is trimmed at the front

indicators.note: A trim takes a slice off, and taking it off the front removes the opening letter.

parts.note: a swatch is a sample of cloth, and its leading S is trimmed away

explanation.walkthrough: Tailoring is all over this clue and none of it matters: the sample and the answer differ by a single letter, which is the entire mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: View → WATCH: to watch is to keep your eyes on something as it happens, and 'view' is the same verb in a slightly more formal register.

clue.text: Sink in which neon reflected?

indicators.note: A reflection shows a thing the other way round, so its letters are read from the far end back.

parts.note: neon is one of the noble gases, and it is turned round

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: it owns up to the fact that naming neon is definition by example, one member standing in for the whole family.
explanation.definitionFit: Sink → SAG: a shelf that sags has sunk in the middle, so both words describe something dropping slowly under its own weight.

clue.text: Last song performed in Moscow, it shows sincerity

indicators.note: A song performed is a song given somebody's own arrangement, and an arrangement is what these letters are getting.

parts.note: eight letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: Gorbachev's word reached English in the 1980s alongside perestroika, and the definition here is a whole phrase: it places the answer in Russia and glosses it at once.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian word means openness — the Soviet policy of saying out loud what the state had been hiding — so the phrase both locates it and translates it.

clue.text: 17, you say, in type of carriage coming back

indicators.note: Said as a word, 'you' is the name of a single letter, and that letter is what the clue wants written down.
An across entry that comes back runs right to left, so these letters go into the grid reversed.

parts.note: a drag is a four-horse coach, and it is turned round

indicators.note: What is named before this goes inside, so the words after it have to open up and take it.

parts.note: the letter U is called exactly what the word 'you' sounds like

explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference is the kindest clue in the grid once its partner is solved. A drag really is a carriage: the four-in-hand coach a Victorian gentleman drove himself.
explanation.definitionFit: 17 across is WATCH, and a guard is a watch in the old sense: the man posted to keep watch, whether a sentry or the one riding the train.

clue.text: Three articles by mother providing curse

parts.note: English has exactly three articles — AN, A and THE — and all three are used, in that order
ma is mother

explanation.walkthrough: Counting is the solve: English has only three articles, and setting them end to end gets you six of the eight letters before the clue asks for anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: curse → ANATHEMA: an anathema was the Church's formal curse of excommunication, and the word now means anything a person utterly detests.

clue.text: Peer from jet, disregarding old ship

indicators.note: To disregard a thing is to take no account of it, so the letter named next is left out of the word in front.

parts.note: a douche is a jet of water, straight from the French for a shower
O is the usual abbreviation for old, and it is the letter dropped
SS is the steamship prefix on a vessel's name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' is the spurt of water, not the aircraft and not the black stone, and that is where the clue does all of its hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: Peer → DUCHESS: a duchess holds the highest rank below royalty in the peerage, so 'peer' names her by the class of title rather than by the masculine word.

clue.text: Bad luck if it's hard

definitions.meaning: read as ordinary English this is somebody commiserating, which is the sense the surface pushes you towards
the qualifier is the point: put 'hard' in front of the answer and you have the old exclamation of rueful sympathy

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here. The clue works by naming a foodstuff that only means bad luck while one particular adjective is standing in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Hard cheese' is the British idiom for tough luck, so the answer carries that meaning only while the adjective is attached to it.

clue.text: One that displays useless lot

definitions.meaning: the agent noun for someone who exhibits or displays something, formed by adding '-er' to the base verb
British slang for a hopeless, disorganised bunch — the kind of insult barked at a chaotic team

explanation.walkthrough: The two halves are not even pronounced alike: the one who shows rhymes with 'lower', the hopeless lot with 'power'. Only the spelling is shared, which is all this type needs.
explanation.definitionFit: One that displays → SHOWER: the agent noun off the verb 'show'; useless lot → SHOWER: army slang for a rabble, shouted at a team playing badly.

clue.text: Sky-high price of cockney's locks sounds reasonable

parts.note: locks are hair, and the cockney's version has lost its aitch

indicators.note: What a word sounds like is not always how it is written, so the spelling that goes in the grid is the other one.

parts.note: a reasonable price is a fair one, and 'fair' is what you hear — the grid takes the other spelling

explanation.walkthrough: Two dialect tricks in one sentence: the dropped aitch, and a fair/fare pair that is among the crossword's favourite soundalikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sky-high price → AIRFARE: an airfare is what you pay to fly, so 'sky-high' points at the air rather than at the size of the bill.

clue.text: Directions with extra finally given after short arm bowl

indicators.note: given after means the directions and final letter come behind the shortened arm
short means the word arm loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written before shortening
E and N are the compass points east and north

indicators.note: finally asks for the last letter of extra

parts.note: last letter of extra

explanation.surface: Instructions for a craft project or cricket delivery: bowl with a short arm.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowl is a cricket verb in the surface, but the definition is the noun: a stadium.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl is a large stadium with tiered seating, an arena for sport or performance.

clue.text: Adams entertaining republican soldiers

definitions.note: An army is one body while 'soldiers' is plural: the definition names the people who make it up, which is the normal way to clue a collective noun.

indicators.note: To entertain a guest is to have them inside the house, so this word takes the letter in among its own.

parts.note: Amy Adams, the actress, supplies the first name
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.walkthrough: A surname on its own is often a first name in disguise, and 'republican' sitting next to Adams points you firmly at Gerry rather than at Amy.
explanation.definitionFit: soldiers → ARMY: an army is a nation's whole land force, so the definition names it by the people in it rather than by the institution.

clue.text: Possession of pier shown to be condemned

indicators.note: A building condemned is one due to be pulled down, and what has been pulled down goes back up in another arrangement.

parts.note: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: Seaside piers really do get condemned, so nothing in the sentence announces itself as an instruction — which is what makes this anagram so hard to spot at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Possession → OWNERSHIP: ownership is the legal fact of owning something, and 'possession' is the everyday word for that same relation between a person and property.

clue.text: A bit funny Penny's missing something needed for toilet

indicators.note: What is missing has gone from where it was, so the letter named just before it comes out of the word.

parts.note: droll is funny in a dry, mild way
the old penny was d, and that is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The old penny was d, from the Roman denarius, which is why 'penny' in a clue so often means a letter that looks nothing like a P.
explanation.definitionFit: something needed for toilet → ROLL: 'toilet roll' is so fixed a phrase that naming the room is enough to fetch the other half of it.

clue.text: Yearn to stick close to fiancée

parts.note: to stick a notice up is to pin it

indicators.note: The close of a word is where it ends, so this takes the final letter of whatever follows.

parts.note: the last letter of FIANCÉE

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick close to' reads as one phrase about devotion and the clue cuts straight through the middle of it. The tree has nothing to do with anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Yearn → PINE: to pine for somebody is to long for them so badly it wears you away, which is 'yearn' with an edge of wasting.

clue.text: One packing essential cape that's showing mould

definitions.note: The answer is a noun naming the state, while 'showing mould' is a participle phrase describing what a musty thing does — the quality defined by its symptom.

indicators.note: To pack something is to push it in among other things, so this letter is pushed in between the two words that follow it.

parts.note: an essential is a must, the thing you cannot do without
a ness is a headland or cape — Dungeness, Sheerness
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Must' is doing two jobs at once: the essential the clue asks for, and the old word for the very smell of a damp shut-up room. That is the neatest touch here.
explanation.definitionFit: showing mould → MUSTINESS: mustiness is the stale damp smell of a room nobody has opened for years, which is what mould in the walls produces.

clue.text: Colour in retrospective Tarantino melodrama

indicators.note: The answer is sitting in the words that follow rather than being spelt out by them.
A retrospective looks back over what has gone before, so these letters are read from the far end backwards.

parts.note: the run straddles the gap in tarantiNO MELodrama, waiting to be turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' is doing double duty: a film season on the surface, and the instruction to read backwards underneath. Lemon here is the pale yellow, not the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Colour → LEMON: lemon names the pale yellow of the fruit's skin, one of the many colours English takes straight from a food.
